headline: How can carriers respond to overcapacity?
noFigure: No sourced figure yet: Req 5 owner to add

responses.title: Fleet management
responses.line: Adjust vessel deployment and charter commitments.
points: Fleet redeployment: shift vessels towards routes with stronger cargo demand
Charter adjustment: reduce chartered capacity when contracts permit
Lay-up: temporarily withdraw vessels from active service
Vessel-size adjustment: match deployed capacity to route demand
Enough total capacity can still mean an imbalance on single routes

responses.title: Slow steaming
responses.line: Reduce speed to absorb effective capacity and save fuel.
points: Fuel use rises steeply with speed (simplified cube rule)
Slower rotations absorb excess capacity: ships take longer per loop
Trade-off: longer transit times, and more ships for the same weekly frequency

responses.title: Scrapping
responses.line: Permanently remove older vessels, to reduce fleet supply.
points: Owner offers the ship, a broker circulates it, demolition buyers bid, the yard recycles it
Scrap value = lightweight tonnage × scrap price per LWT
Lay-up is temporary; scrapping is permanent
Limits: owners keep ships that still pay, and newbuilds offset the removals

responses.title: Network design
responses.line: Optimise routes, port calls and vessel allocation.
points: Optimise routes, service loops and port rotations
Match vessel size and frequency to cargo demand
Improve vessel utilisation and operational efficiency

responses.title: Consolidation
responses.line: Combine overlapping services and coordinate capacity.
points: Combine overlapping or underutilised services and reduce duplicated capacity
Coordinate vessel deployment between carriers, keep transit times and reliability
Example: Hapag-Lloyd and Maersk's Gemini Cooperation (2025)
responses.close: Managing overcapacity is not simply about removing ships. Carriers balance four goals: control capacity, competitive transit times, lower costs, reliable service.
